title: Competing Deadlines
text: Your deadlines today: the report, due at 5 PM. Also a snack, due now. A diaper, overdue. A hug, due immediately, with interest. Only one of these was assigned by an adult.

choices.label: Clear the toddler queue first: snack, diaper, hug

outcomes.text: Snack: delivered. Diaper: resolved. Hug: received, reviewed, approved. {kid} lets you work for 51 straight minutes. You get more done than you did all of Monday.
Snack, diaper, hug. Then a second hug, unscheduled. Then a third. The report is at 2%. The hugs are at 300%.

choices.label: Work first. They can wait. (They cannot wait.)

outcomes.text: You open the report. {kid} escalates the diaper issue in person, on your lap, in a way that can't be ignored. You're at 0% and you need a shower.
Somehow, they wait. They sit beside you "working" on a closed calculator for 25 minutes. You hit 30%. They hit nothing. You both feel productive.

choices.label: Ask {partner}: "Can you take {kid} till 10?"

outcomes.text: {partner} closes their laptop and leaves with {kid} and a sippy cup. They don't say "you owe me." Their posture says it for them.
"I have the all-hands at 10." They do. They've mentioned it four times this week. You both stand in the hallway, holding opposite ends of the same tiredness.

title: Last Call for Coffee
text: The report needs two more hours of brain. You have about twenty minutes left. It's mid-afternoon: last call for coffee, if you'd like to sleep tonight.

choices.label: Fourth coffee. Tonight is tomorrow's problem.

outcomes.text: You type with the focus of a jewel thief. The report jumps to 70%. At 11 PM you'll be wide awake, narrating it to {partner}, who is asleep.
Coffee four hits like a fire alarm. You write 900 words in 20 minutes. Later you'll reread them. They're mostly about coffee.

choices.label: Ask {partner} to take {kid} for an hour

outcomes.text: They take {kid} to the park. You write in a silent house, then sit very still for six minutes, listening to the fridge hum. It sounds like the ocean.
"I've got a 3:30." It's on the shared calendar, in the color you agreed was theirs. You finish the report with {kid} on your shoulders, steering your head.

choices.label: Splash your face. Finish it on willpower.

outcomes.text: It's good, actually. You'd celebrate, but standing up makes the room tilt, so you celebrate sitting down, quietly, with a cracker.

title: Due at 5
text: The report is 80% done and due at 5, which is suddenly very soon. {kid} has gone behind the curtain to poop and needs you to hold their hand. They have never been in less of a hurry.

choices.label: Hold the hand. Type with the other one.

outcomes.text: You type one-handed, at arm's length, around a curtain, while {kid} narrates. 91%. 96%. Done. Your cursor is on Send. From behind the curtain: "{ME}! I'm DONE!"

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. They can poop to corduroy.

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings about patience. {kid} takes the advice. You write like the building is on fire and hit send as the credits roll. You'll take the meltdown. You'd take ten.
{kid} finishes, emerges and wants to watch the rest on your lap, holding your typing hand. The last paragraph goes in typed with one finger.

choices.label: Send it at 80%. "Happy to discuss!"

outcomes.text: "Happy to discuss!" is corporate for "I know." Trent replies with a thumbs-up and nothing else. A thumbs-up can mean anything. This one means Monday.
Trent replies at once: "honestly the first 80% is the part people read." You've been doing the last 20% for nothing your entire career.

choices.label: Hit send. You're somehow ahead.

outcomes.text: Sent. Early. You sit there for a full minute, unsure what people do with spare time. {kid} shows you: you build a tower and knock it down until five o'clock.

title: Send or Change
text: Your cursor is on Send. From behind the curtain: "{ME}! I'm DONE! CHANGE ME!" This is a two-hand diaper. You have one free hand, two jobs and about five seconds.

choices.label: Click Send, then sprint

outcomes.text: Click. Sent. You sprint. Behind the curtain, {kid} has attempted to change their own diaper. The attempt was ambitious. The curtain is involved.
Click. Wrong button. The report goes to 31 people, on time, with your draft text to {partner} still in the body: "brb, wiping."

choices.label: Change first. The report can wait 90 seconds.

outcomes.text: Change, wash, back at the laptop with 40 seconds to spare. Sent. You stand in the kitchen with clean hands and a pounding heart: a person who did two jobs at once.
Change, wash, back at the laptop one minute too late. Trent replies "no worries!" with an exclamation point that will keep you up tonight.

choices.label: Freeze

outcomes.text: You stand frozen between the laptop and the curtain. {kid} waddles out, diaper at the ankles, and presses Send for you. With their hand. That hand. Sent, on time, technically.

title: With Intent
text: {kid} is walking toward you, one finger extended, with tremendous purpose. That finger has just been in their eye, then the butter, then the remote. It is headed for your mouth.

choices.label: Intercept: "UP HIGH!"

outcomes.text: The finger becomes a palm, the palm becomes a high five, and the germs land somewhere you can wash. {kid} is thrilled. You're 40% hand sanitizer by now anyway.
"Up high!" Too slow. The finger goes up your nose instead. Nobody has ever been so pleased with a miss.

choices.label: Offer your elbow, like a doctor

outcomes.text: {kid} pokes the elbow, satisfied, and wanders off to touch the TV with the same finger. The TV is part of this now.
{kid} pokes the elbow, considers it and, unsatisfied, goes for your ear.

choices.label: Freeze

outcomes.text: The finger arrives. It touches your bottom lip, gently, like a blessing. "Boop," says {kid}. You will think about the remote for the rest of the day.

title: 1,100 Square Feet
text: Hour seven at home. The house is 1,100 square feet and you've been in every one of them, with {kid}, at least 40 times. You've read the truck book 19 times. You can do it with your eyes closed. You have.

choices.label: Blanket fort. Commit to the bit.

outcomes.text: Four chairs, every blanket you own and a flashlight. Inside, {kid} whispers like you're both hiding from someone. You stay in there much longer than you meant to.
The fort collapses at minute three and becomes "the cave." The cave is better. The cave has your pillow and the crackers. You live in the cave now.

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. Just one.

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings about rainy days. You sit on the kitchen floor eating cold pasta out of the container, which is your version of a spa.

choices.label: Leave the house. Anywhere. The hardware store.

outcomes.text: {kid} walks the aisles in awe of the lumber. You buy one hinge for no reason. It's the best outing you've had all year, and it cost $2.14.
{kid} touches every doorknob in the doorknob aisle, with intent. You remember why you were home. The cashier wipes the counter before you've left it.

choices.label: "Quiet time. You play. I lie on the floor."

outcomes.text: They play beside you, narrating, for 14 whole minutes. You stare at the ceiling. It's the best meeting you've had all week.
Quiet time lasts 90 seconds. Then it becomes loud time, on your stomach, with a drum.

title: Wash Everything on Hot
text: Daycare's email says to wash "all bedding, towels and soft toys" on hot. Bun-Bun is a soft toy. Bun-Bun has never been washed. Bun-Bun has a smell {kid} describes as "home."

choices.label: Every load. Bun-Bun too.

outcomes.text: Four loads. {kid} watches Bun-Bun tumble in the dryer window, both palms on the glass. Bun-Bun comes out warm, fluffy and, according to {kid}, "wrong."
Bun-Bun survives the hot wash. One ear does not. {kid} holds the ear up to you like a lost tooth. You get out the sewing kit you've never opened.

choices.label: Text {partner}: laundry tonight is theirs

outcomes.text: "On it." Four loads after bedtime, folded, Bun-Bun included. You find Bun-Bun on your pillow at 10 PM, still warm. You're not crying. It's the steam.
"I did laundry Sunday." It was one load, of their gym clothes. You don't say that. You think it, at a volume they can probably hear.

choices.label: Just the sheets. Bun-Bun stays feral.

outcomes.text: Sheets on hot. Bun-Bun stays fragrant and untouched. If daycare asks, Bun-Bun was washed, and you will lie to a teacher's face.

title: The Snot Straw
text: {kid} doesn't have pink eye. {kid} has a bonus cold. You own the mouth-powered nasal aspirator: one end goes in their nose, the other end goes in your mouth. There's a filter. You've read about it four times.

choices.label: Use the snot straw. Trust the filter.

outcomes.text: It works. It's horrifying. It works. {kid} won't forgive you until dinner, but they'll breathe through their nose tonight, which means you might sleep.
It works so well you can hear it working. You'll hear it again at 3 AM, in your memory, uninvited.

choices.label: Let it run. Embrace the glaze.

outcomes.text: By lunch, every surface in the house has been personally initialed.
{kid} discovers that a sleeve works as well as a tissue. Your sleeve. You're wearing it. They're very polite about it.

choices.label: Tissues, a song and enormous patience

outcomes.text: You invent a song about noses. It has four verses. They let you wipe on verse three. Partial credit.
You invent a nose song. {kid} loves it so much they won't let you wipe until you've sung it nine more times. The nose is still running. So is the song.

title: Teething?
text: {partner} checks in from work.

messages.text: they cried because their sock was "too yellow"

choices.label: "Everything is teething. The economy is teething."

outcomes.text: {partner} laughs at their desk hard enough that someone asks if they're okay. Then they do something better than laugh.

chat.text: getting teething rings on the way home. and a toaster

choices.label: "Or maybe they're just like this?"

outcomes.text: You both sit with that, in separate buildings, for a long time.

chat.text: what if they're just like this

outcomes.text: That's not teething. That's slander. It's also accurate. You eat a granola bar and reconsider everything.

chat.text: they're like you when you're hungry

choices.label: Frozen spoon, cold hands, your full attention

outcomes.text: A frozen spoon, then your cold knuckle, then the spoon again. Twenty minutes later {kid} is chewing slowly, eyes heavy, humming. You report back.
The spoon works until {kid} realizes it's a spoon, at which point it becomes a drumstick and the coffee table becomes a drum.

title: The Bite
text: Mid-cuddle, {kid} bites your shoulder. Not a nibble: a molar-assisted chomp, with eye contact. Then a giggle, because your face just did something it has never done before.

choices.label: Calm voice: "Ouch. Teeth are for the teether."

outcomes.text: You swap your shoulder for a cold teether and say it in the voice of a flight attendant during turbulence. They chomp the teether instead. Lesson received, for about ten minutes.
They bite the teether, then you, then the teether, as if comparing. You come second. It stings in a whole new way.

choices.label: Make a big, wounded noise

outcomes.text: It's the funniest thing that has ever happened. They bite again, for an encore. The encore gets a [BLEEP]. You're a squeaky toy with a mortgage now.
Your noise is so big that {kid} pats your shoulder, very gently, to apologize. Then bites it again, very gently. It's an apology. It's also a bite.

choices.label: Frozen teether plus a pouch. Buy the peace.

outcomes.text: One cold ring, one $2.99 pouch. Silence, chewing, a small sigh from both of you. Then the pouch gets squeezed into the couch. Your shoulder now has a dental record.

title: Bib Number Seven
text: Bib number seven. The drool is industrial. {kid}'s chin is red and chapped, your shoulder is damp, and the couch has a wet patch the shape of a small country.

choices.label: Chin balm after every single wipe

outcomes.text: You apply balm eleven times. By the eleventh, {kid} lifts their chin for it, like a boxer between rounds. The red fades. Your respect for boxing trainers grows.

choices.label: Text {partner}: more bibs, the good balm

outcomes.text: They come home with a 10-pack of bibs and the good balm, the one in the tin, bought without a single follow-up question. You consider proposing again.
"What kind of bibs?" "The bib kind." They come home with one bib. It has a lobster on it and says SHELL YEAH. Technically, a bib.

choices.label: Let it drip. You live in a swamp now.

outcomes.text: You stop fighting it. Everything you own is slightly damp. The couch patch is now a large country, with a coastline and a capital.
{kid} discovers that drool will stick a cracker to a window. There are nine crackers on the window. You leave them up. It's a gallery.

title: "In My Day"
text: {kid} is gnawing the table leg. Grandma sips some tea and says, "In my day, we put a little whiskey on your gums, and you slept like a lamb." A long look at you. "And you turned out fine." A pause. Too long.

choices.label: Cite the pediatrician like scripture

outcomes.text: You explain, calmly, that nobody puts whiskey on a toddler now. Grandma nods. "Oh, I know. I'm not going to DO it. I'm just saying it worked." The bottle stays shut. The point stays on the table.
You cite the pediatrician, the guidelines and a pamphlet. Grandma reads the entire pamphlet, then hands it back: "Lovely font." {partner} has to leave the room.

choices.label: "Did it work, though?"

outcomes.text: "Oh, no," says Grandma. "You screamed for two years." A sip of tea. "But we slept."
"Like a charm." A sip of tea. "Of course, you also didn't talk until you were four." From the doorway, {partner}: "That explains a lot."

choices.label: Let Grandma take over. Nap face-down.

outcomes.text: You sleep 58 minutes. You wake to a toddler who has eaten three cookies and learned a new word. You don't know which word. Daycare will tell you.
You wake in a panic. The house is silent. {kid} is asleep in the crib. Grandma, from the couch: "I just put them down, dear." Just put them down. You've never been so rested or so insulted.

title: Grandma Has Posted
text: Grandma has posted 41 photos of today. Number 23: {kid} eating spaghetti with both fists, captioned "Somebody's parents let them eat like THIS 😂." It has 88 likes. Three are from the daycare group chat.

choices.label: Call Grandma. Request a takedown. Kindly.

outcomes.text: It comes down. A new post goes up: "Not allowed to share the spaghetti one 🙄." It has more likes than the spaghetti.
"Of course, sweetheart," says Grandma, and takes it down, in a voice so sincere you check it for traps. There are no traps. You're too tired to trust that.

choices.label: Comment: "Best day ever!! ❤️❤️❤️"

outcomes.text: Spin control. Two parents like your comment. One replies "lol the spaghetti 😂." You've made it a thread. Threads are forever.
Grandma replies: "Best day ever because GRANDMA was here!! 😘" The likes double. You've been out-posted by someone who types with one finger.

choices.label: Screenshot it to {partner}

outcomes.text: "LOL. Honestly, the spaghetti looks great." A small, private laugh between the two people who actually run this place.
"Well, DID you let them eat like that?" You did. They know you did. You set the phone face-down, very gently, like it might go off.

title: "You Cut Them THAT Way"
text: At dinner, Grandma watches {partner} cut {kid}'s noodles into small, sensible pieces. "Oh," Grandma says, to no one, to everyone. "You cut them THAT way." The knife stops.

choices.label: "They cut them perfectly."

outcomes.text: Grandma raises both hands, the picture of innocence. The knife resumes. Later, the family group chat learns you've been "very sensitive lately."
"Oh, I'm sure they do," says Grandma, with a warmth that has teeth. The knife resumes. The tone does not.

choices.label: Laugh along. They do cut them a bit small.

outcomes.text: Grandma beams. The knife stays very still. You'll hear about this at 10:40 PM, in a whisper, in the dark.
Everyone laughs. {partner} laughs a little too long, then cuts the next noodle into one enormous piece, while maintaining eye contact with you.

choices.label: Ask Grandma about the knee. All of it.

outcomes.text: Thirty minutes on the knee: the surgeon, the parking, the physical therapist who "isn't a real doctor." {partner} finishes dinner in peace and squeezes your hand under the table.
The knee, then the other knee, then a neighbor's hip. {partner} mouths "thank you," then "sorry," then "I love you," then nothing. They've fallen asleep sitting up.

title: Grandma Brought a Gift
text: Grandma brought a gift: a toy saxophone. It plays the same eight notes of jazz at 94 decibels and has no off switch. Grandma leaves Sunday. The saxophone does not.

choices.label: "Wow! Thank you!" Smile through the jazz.

outcomes.text: You smile through 31 renditions. Grandma glows. {kid} glows. Your left eye does a thing. It will keep doing the thing until Sunday.
Your "Wow!" is so convincing that Grandma reaches into the bag again. "I knew you'd love it. That's why I got the drum."

choices.label: Remove the batteries tonight. Blame the factory.

outcomes.text: Surgery at 9 PM with a tiny screwdriver. In the morning, {kid} blows into a silent saxophone and looks at you. Not at the saxophone. At you.
Batteries out. Silence. Then you learn it has a backup battery, for memory. At 2 AM it plays the eight notes once, softly. Just once. To let you know.

choices.label: Pack it in Grandma's suitcase. "Oops."

outcomes.text: Two days later, a text: "Found the saxophone in my bag! Silly me! Bringing it back next visit 🎷" It's coming back. It always comes back.
Grandma finds it while packing and hands it back with a wink. "You almost lost this!" Grandma knows. Grandma has always known.

title: False Alarm #9
text: "I NEED TO GO POTTY!" This could be the breakthrough. It could also be false alarm number nine since lunch. You can't tell anymore. Neither can they.

choices.label: Sprint. Carry them under one arm, horizontally.

outcomes.text: SUCCESS. You throw a three-minute celebration with a dance and a sticker. You have never been prouder of anything, including your career.
False alarm. Then a real alarm, ninety seconds later, on the rug you'd just decided was safe.

choices.label: "Are you SURE?"

outcomes.text: They were sure.
They weren't sure. They wanted to flush. Seven times. They wave goodbye to each flush like it's leaving on a cruise.

choices.label: Diaper back on. Day 3 is a social construct.

outcomes.text: Nobody has to know. Everybody will know. The internet said you'd be tempted, and the internet, for once, was right.

title: Sticker Inflation
text: The deal was one sticker per potty. {kid} has renegotiated: two stickers, a cracker and "the big song." The chart on the fridge looks like a currency in collapse.

choices.label: Hold the line: one sticker, no song

outcomes.text: They accept the terms, sulk and go anyway. One sticker. You feel like a central banker who did the hard thing.
{kid} goes on strike. The strike takes place on the kitchen floor, with eye contact, and it is not a dry strike.

choices.label: Two stickers and a cracker. Inflation is real.

outcomes.text: It works too well. They now go in tiny installments, for maximum stickers. Nine before lunch. You're out of dinosaurs and down to the dentist's smiley faces.

choices.label: Full potty parade for every success

outcomes.text: You march. You sing. You bang a pot with a wooden spoon. They're so into it they go twice. You're so into it you pull something in your hip.
The parade is such a hit that {kid} now demands one for things that aren't potty. A parade for socks. A parade for a sneeze. You're the band now.

title: Bare-Bottom Afternoon
text: The method says: no pants, lots of water, watch for "the signs." {kid} is pantsless, hydrated and showing the signs either constantly or never. You've watched a small bottom for 40 minutes like a lighthouse keeper.

choices.label: Keep watching. Potty every 20 minutes.

outcomes.text: Ding. Sprint. Success! You cheer so loudly a dog two houses down joins in. {kid} takes a bow, which, given the outfit, is a lot.
Between timers: the couch. The good couch. Twelve seconds after the last trip, with total confidence.

choices.label: Sunshine Sing-Along. Stillness helps, right?

outcomes.text: The man in corduroy sings about rain. {kid} sits perfectly still on the couch. Stillness, it turns out, is exactly when it happens. The cushion cover goes in the wash.

choices.label: Towels on every surface. Every one.

outcomes.text: Fourteen towels. The living room looks like a spa that's given up. It works: everything lands on terry cloth. You now have fourteen towels to wash.
Fourteen towels. {kid} finds the one square foot with no towel on it and uses it, precisely, as if aiming.

title: The Auto-Flush
text: A public restroom. {kid} is finally on the big toilet. Behind them, the auto-flush sensor blinks red. It's thinking about it. You have about five seconds.

choices.label: Palm over the sensor. Hold.

outcomes.text: You hold your palm over the sensor for four minutes, bent like a question mark, whispering encouragement. Success. You'll never get the feeling back in that arm.
You cover the sensor. It flushes anyway, out of spite. {kid} levitates. They'll be telling this story at 30.

choices.label: Sticky note over it. You came prepared.

outcomes.text: The veteran's move. The note goes on and the sensor goes blind. {kid} pees in peace while you stand guard at the stall door, arms crossed, terrifying.
You reach into the bag for the sticky notes and find a receipt, a crayon and a single raisin. The sensor decides for you.

choices.label: Freeze

outcomes.text: WHOOSH. {kid} is off the toilet and out of the stall in one motion, pantsless, telling the whole restroom "THE POTTY TRIED TO EAT ME." Potty training has been pushed to spring.

title: The Going-Out Shirt
text: Your going-out shirt has been in a drawer since spring. It has a crease like a folded map, a stain like a smaller map and, as of four minutes ago, a toddler wearing it as a cape.

choices.label: Iron it. Treat the stain. Be a person.

outcomes.text: Stain stick, steam, a second pass. It looks almost new in low light, which the restaurant will provide. You hold it up like a trophy you ironed yourself.
It's perfect. You hang it on the door. When you come back, the cape has returned, on {kid}, who is now Captain Date Night and will not be taking questions.

choices.label: Dryer, damp towel, ten minutes. Pray.

outcomes.text: The crease is 60% gone. The stain is now baked in, permanently. You'll keep an arm over it all night like a nervous senator.
The crease is gone. So are two sizes. It's a crop top now. You're wearing it anyway. It's a choice.

choices.label: Wear the sweater. The sweater is always fine.

outcomes.text: The sweater has seen four Fridays like this one. {partner} says, "The sweater, huh?" in a voice that's either fond or not. You don't ask which.
{partner} walks in wearing their own sweater. The same sweater. You bought them as a set in 2021 and swore you'd never wear them together. Tonight, you do.

title: Reservation Confirmed
text: {partner} texts: "Confirmed for 7:30!! 🎉" Then: "I could leave at 3:30 so you can rest? I'd have to log back on later, but." The "but" just sits there. It's a real offer. It's also a real but.

choices.label: "Yes. Please. Come home."

outcomes.text: They're home by 4. You lie in a dark room for 40 minutes, charging. When you get up, {kid} has "helped" fold the laundry, which means unfolded it.
They're home at 4:40 and back on the laptop by 4:45. "I'm here, though!" they say, from behind a screen. Technically, they are.

choices.label: "I've got it. Finish your day."

outcomes.text: You've got it. You absolutely have it. At 4:30 you're on the floor looking for a shoe, and you have it, and {partner} sends a heart, and that has to count for something.
You have it until 4:52, when you text "actually." They're home by 5:10 with a pizza and zero questions. The date hasn't started, and it's already the most romantic thing that will happen tonight.

choices.label: "Only if you bring the good cheese."

outcomes.text: They arrive at 3:50 with the expensive cheese and the crackers that come in a box with a window. You eat it standing up in the kitchen, together: an appetizer for the appetizer.
They arrive at 3:50 with "cheese": a family-size bag of string cheese. It's the thought that counts. The thought was "string cheese."

title: Cleaning for a Teenager
text: The sitter arrives in five hours. The sitter is 16 and will notice nothing. You are, nonetheless, about to clean the entire house for a 16-year-old.

choices.label: Clean everything. You have standards (for a teen).

outcomes.text: The bathroom, the counters and a drawer the sitter will never open. At 7, the sitter walks in, looks at nothing and says, "Cute house." You'll take it.
You clean for 45 minutes. {kid} follows two steps behind, un-cleaning at exactly the same speed. You end where you began, but sweatier.

choices.label: Close every door. The house is one room now.

outcomes.text: Bedroom: closed. Laundry room: closed. Office: closed. The sitter will think you live in a kitchen with a couch. You basically do.
Doors closed. At 7:20 the sitter texts, "which door is the bathroom 😅" They've opened them all. They've seen everything.

choices.label: Rest instead. Energy is the real outfit.

outcomes.text: You lie down "for ten minutes" and get up at 1:40, rested and certain you never fell asleep. The house is a disaster. You are a new person in it.
